scenes.narration: Four cables between two switches. But only one actually carries traffic. The rest are switched off to avoid a loop. What a waste.

scenes.heading: Merging the tollbooths
scenes.narration: Imagine four tollbooths into the same city. Spanning tree closes three of them to stop loops. EtherChannel merges all four into one super booth with four lanes. To the rest of the network, it looks like a single link. Cars are assigned a lane by a hash of who they are and where they're going. So one conversation always stays in one lane, and nothing arrives out of order.

scenes.heading: Negotiating the bundle
scenes.narration: There are two ways to negotiate a bundle. L A C P is the open standard, with modes active and passive. Cisco has its own version, with modes desirable and auto. You can also force it with mode on, but nothing checks the other side.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three things to watch. Traffic isn't shared packet by packet. It's hashed per flow. Two active L A C P ports do form a bundle. And every link in the bundle must match on speed and duplex.

items.wrong: Traffic is shared packet by packet
items.right: A hash keeps each flow on one link

items.wrong: LACP active needs passive on the other end

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. EtherChannel bundles several links into one, for more speed and backup. L A C P is the standard, and active on both ends works well. Spanning tree sees one link, so nothing gets blocked. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva EtherChannel lab.

points.t: LACP: use active on both ends
STP sees one link, nothing is blocked
